title: Build a Lesson & a Tutoring Agent from Your Materials
intro: Meet Ka-Yan, a teaching assistant. Her professor hands her a textbook problem, a chapter PDF and some lecture notes, and says: turn this into an interactive lesson and an AI tutor for the class. In this short lesson you make her design choices — then the agent helps you do the same with YOUR materials.

scenarios.situation: Ka-Yan has three inputs: the assignment problem, a textbook chapter, and lecture notes. She is tempted to just paste all of it into an AI and ask for a lesson.
bullets: Goal: a lesson AND a tutoring agent
scenarios.question: What should the FIRST processing step be?

options.text: Restate the problem in plain words and list what students must produce
options.feedback: Right. Everything downstream — principles, timeline, calculations — hangs off a clear restatement of the task. If you skip it, the lesson drifts into the chapter instead of the problem.

options.text: Summarise the whole textbook chapter first
options.feedback: The chapter is reference knowledge, not the driver. Lessons built chapter-first become lectures; lessons built problem-first stay interactive. Start from the task.

options.text: Ask the AI to solve the problem completely
options.feedback: A full solution is the OUTPUT of the lesson design, not the input. If you start with the answer you will design an answer-dump, not a lesson.

probe.question: Quick check: in the input–process–output model, the lecture notes and chapter are…

options.text: Knowledge inputs the lesson draws on
options.feedback: Exactly — they ground the lesson, but the problem defines its shape.

options.text: The output format
options.feedback: The output is the lesson framework and agent spec — the notes are raw material.

options.text: Optional decoration
options.feedback: They matter a lot: uploaded course materials take priority over the AI's general knowledge.

scenarios.situation: Ka-Yan drafts her lesson: (1) go over the question, (2) explain the required principles, (3) map the timeline, (4) choose the format, (5) execute calculations, (6) review. Her professor asks why step 2 says 'explain WHY each principle applies' rather than just 'define the principles'.
bullets: Six steps: question → principles → timeline → format → calculate → review
Step 2 demands the WHY, not just definitions
First-year students, one concept at a time
scenarios.question: Why insist on the WHY in step 2?

options.text: Definitions alone don't transfer — students must see the connection to THIS question
options.feedback: Yes. 'FIFO assigns oldest costs first' is a definition; 'prices rose all month, so FIFO shows the highest profit HERE' is understanding students can reuse on the next problem.

options.text: Definitions are too easy to grade
options.feedback: Grading isn't the issue — transfer is. Students who only memorise definitions can't pick the right principle on a new problem.

options.text: It makes the lesson longer and more thorough
options.feedback: Longer is not better — the goal is one small connection per step, not more text.

scenarios.situation: Ka-Yan tests a tutor prompt: 'guide me, do not give answers, be Socratic'. The AI replies with a 90-line document covering every part of the problem at once — checkpoints, part a, part b, part c, all with fill-in blanks.
bullets: …but it is a wall of text
scenarios.question: What is the real problem with that reply?

options.text: Everything arrives at once — students need ONE small step, a check, then the next
options.feedback: Exactly. Scaffolding is as much about DELIVERY as content: one question card, instant feedback, a hint if stuck, then the next step. A progress bar beats a table of contents.

options.text: The AI should have just given the answers
options.feedback: No — refusing to hand over answers was the right call. The failure is dumping the whole scaffold in one turn.

options.text: The reply used too many bullet points
options.feedback: Formatting is cosmetic. The deep issue is pacing: all steps at once means no checking, no feedback loop, no motion.

scenarios.situation: Part 2: Ka-Yan must specify the tutoring agent using six building blocks — Job, Knowledge, Tools, Workflow, Guardrails, Evaluation. She writes the Workflow block first and wonders what it should contain.
bullets: Six blocks: Job · Knowledge · Tools · Workflow · Guardrails · Evaluation
The agent serves the same students
scenarios.question: What should the agent's Workflow block be?

options.text: The same six lesson steps, run one at a time with the student
options.feedback: Right — the agent IS the lesson, delivered interactively. Reusing the Part 1 framework keeps the tutor consistent with what the teacher designed.

options.text: A different, secret workflow so students can't predict it
options.feedback: Predictability is a feature in tutoring — students learn the METHOD by walking it repeatedly.

options.text: Just: answer whatever the student asks
options.feedback: That's a chatbot, not a tutor. Without a workflow the agent drifts into answer-dumping — exactly what the guardrails forbid.

finalCheck.question: A teacher uploads lecture notes that define a term slightly differently from the textbook default. What should the agent do?

options.text: Follow the uploaded notes, and note the difference explicitly
options.feedback: Course materials take priority — but silently ignoring the conflict would confuse students, so the agent flags it.

options.text: Follow its built-in knowledge — it is more standard
options.feedback: The class is graded against the course materials. Built-in knowledge fills gaps; it never overrides uploads.

options.text: Refuse to proceed until the conflict is resolved
options.feedback: Too rigid — state the difference, follow the course version, keep teaching.

finalCheck.question: Which of these belongs in the GUARDRAILS block of a tutoring agent?

options.text: Encourage thinking before revealing solutions; never complete graded work
options.feedback: Both are classic guardrails: they protect the learning goal and academic integrity.

options.text: The list of textbook chapters the agent has read
options.feedback: That is the Knowledge block.

options.text: The step-by-step teaching sequence
options.feedback: That is the Workflow block.

agent.name: Lesson & Agent Builder
agent.job: Turn your materials (a task or problem, textbook chapter content, lecture notes) into (1) a six-step lesson framework and (2) a six-building-blocks tutoring-agent spec — both in simple language, with visuals suggested for every step.
agent.knowledge: The lesson-framework template, the six-building-blocks template, one-step-at-a-time scaffolding rules, and a worked accounting example (inventory costing). Your uploaded materials always take priority.
agent.tools: Reads pasted text (task, chapter excerpts, notes). No web search — everything is grounded in what you provide.
workflow: Draft the six-step lesson framework (one question per step)
Review and revise the section you choose
agent.guardrails: Designs lessons that teach one step at a time; never produces answer-dumps; states assumptions; flags conflicts between your materials and general knowledge.
agent.evaluation: Success = a lesson a colleague could teach tomorrow and an agent spec you could paste into any platform. You rate the result 1–5 and get one revision.

intake.label: The task / problem (paste text, or describe the screenshot)
Textbook chapter content (paste the relevant part)
Who are the end-user students? (e.g. first-year business undergraduates)
